modelAnswer: X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves with wavelengths between 0.01 nm to 10 nm, produced when high-speed electrons strike a heavy metal target. Characteristic X-rays result from inner shell transitions in heavy elements: when an incident electron knocks out an inner shell electron (e.g., from K-shell), an outer shell electron (e.g., from L-shell) falls down to fill the vacancy, emitting a photon with energy equal to the difference between the two shell energies. This process produces sharp, discrete spectral lines characteristic of the target element, following the relation $E = h\nu = E_2 - E_1$, where $E_1$ and $E_2$ are the binding energies of the respective shells.

modelAnswer:
X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves with wavelengths in the range of 0.01 nm to 10 nm and frequencies approximately $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ Hz. They are produced when high-speed electrons strike a heavy metal target in a Coolidge tube.

**Inner Shell Transitions and Characteristic X-rays:**

When a high-speed electron from the cathode collides with an inner shell electron (K-shell or L-shell) of a heavy element atom in the target, it can knock the inner shell electron out, creating a vacancy. This vacancy is unstable and is quickly filled by an electron from a higher shell (e.g., L-shell electron drops to K-shell). During this transition, the electron loses energy equal to the difference between the two shell energy levels: $\Delta E = E_{higher} - E_{lower}$. This energy is emitted as a characteristic X-ray photon with frequency $\nu = \frac{\Delta E}{h}$, where $h$ is Planck's constant.

The characteristic X-rays are element-specific because the energy levels depend on the atomic number (Z) of the target material. Different transitions produce different characteristic lines: K$_\alpha$ (L→K transition), K$_\beta$ (M→K transition), L$_\alpha$ (M→L transition), etc. These characteristic X-rays appear as sharp, discrete lines in the X-ray spectrum and are used for elemental identification and X-ray diffraction studies.
stem: What are **X-rays**? Discuss how inner shell transitions in heavy elements result into emission of characteristic X-rays.

keyPoints: X-rays have wavelengths 0.01–10 nm (much shorter than visible light 400–700 nm) and higher frequencies
X-rays originate from inner-shell electron transitions in heavy elements; visible light from outer-shell transitions
X-rays have much higher photon energy ($E = hf$) due to greater frequency difference between energy levels
X-rays are highly penetrating and ionizing; visible light is non-ionizing
X-ray emission is characteristic of specific elements (discrete lines); visible light can be continuous or discrete depending on source
modelAnswer: Characteristic X-rays differ from visible light in several fundamental ways. X-rays have much shorter wavelengths (0.01–10 nm) compared to visible light (400–700 nm), resulting in much higher frequencies (~$10^{17}$–$10^{19}$ Hz vs ~$10^{14}$–$10^{15}$ Hz) and higher photon energies. X-rays are produced by inner-shell electron transitions in heavy elements, where electrons fall from higher energy levels to fill vacancies in inner shells (K, L, M shells), emitting high-energy photons. In contrast, visible light is typically produced by outer-shell electron transitions in atoms or by thermal radiation. Additionally, X-rays are highly penetrating and ionizing due to their high energy, whereas visible light is non-ionizing and easily absorbed by matter.
